column1: In a land swept by typhoons and shaken by earthquakes, how have Japan’s tallest and seemingly flimsiest old buildings - 500 or so wooden pagodas - remained standing for centuries?
column2: 日本常遭台风侵袭和地震撼动。在这片土地上，那些最高、看似最不牢靠的古建筑——约五百座木塔——为何能屹立数百年？

column1: Records show that only two have collapsed during the past 1400 years.
column2: 记录显示，过去一千四百年间，只有两座塔倒塌。

column1: Those that have disappeared were destroyed by fire as a result of lightning or civil war.
column2: 那些已经不复存在的塔，是毁于雷击或内战引起的火灾。

column1: The disastrous Hanshin earthquake in 1995 killed 6,400 people, toppled elevated highways, flattened office blocks and devastated the port area of Kobe.
column2: 1995年的阪神大地震造成6400人死亡，高架公路倾塌，办公楼被夷为平地，神户港区也遭到严重破坏。

column1: Yet it left the magnificent five-storey pagoda at the Toji temple in nearby Kyoto unscathed, though it levelled a number of buildings in the neighbourhood.
column2: 然而，附近京都东寺那座宏伟的五层塔却在地震中毫发无损，尽管周围好些建筑都被夷为平地。

column1: Japanese scholars have been mystified for ages about why these tall, slender buildings are so stable.
column2: 长期以来，日本学者一直不明白，这些高而细长的建筑为何如此稳固。

column1: It was only thirty years ago that the building industry felt confident enough to erect office blocks of steel and reinforced concrete that had more than a dozen floors.
column2: 直到三十年前，建筑业才有足够的信心，用钢材和钢筋混凝土建造超过十二层的办公楼。

column1: With its special shock absorbers to dampen the effect of sudden sideways movements from an earthquake, the thirty-six-storey Kasumigaseki building in central Tokyo - Japan’s first skyscraper - was considered a masterpiece of modern engineering when it was built in 1968.
column2: 专门的减震器可以减轻地震引起的突发横向运动的影响。配有这种装置的霞关大厦位于东京市中心，高三十六层，是日本第一座摩天楼。它在1968年建成时被视为现代工程的杰作。

column1: Yet in 826, with only pegs and wedges to keep his wooden structure upright, the master builder Kobodaishi had no hesitation in sending his majestic Toji pagoda soaring fifty-five metres into the sky - nearly half as high as the Kasumigaseki skyscraper built some eleven centuries later.
column2: 然而早在826年，仅靠木销和楔子保持木结构直立，建筑名匠弘法大师就毫不犹豫地建起了高五十五米、巍然耸立的东寺塔。它的高度接近约一千一百年后建成的霞关大厦的一半。
column8: had no hesitation in|毫不犹豫地做
column11: nearly half as high as|高度接近……的一半
column13: some eleven centuries later|大约十一世纪以后

column1: Clearly, Japanese carpenters of the day knew a few tricks about allowing a building to sway and settle itself rather than fight nature’s forces.
column2: 显然，当时的日本木匠掌握了一些窍门，能让建筑物随之摇摆、再自行恢复稳定，避免与自然力硬抗。
column6: knew a few tricks|掌握一些窍门

column1: But what sort of tricks?
column2: 可到底是什么窍门呢？

column1: The multi-storey pagoda came to Japan from China in the sixth century.
column2: 六世纪，多层佛塔从中国传入日本。

column1: As in China, they were first introduced with Buddhism and were attached to important temples.
column2: 与中国的情况一样，这些塔最初随佛教传入，附属于重要的寺院。

column1: The Chinese built their pagodas in brick or stone, with inner staircases, and used them in later centuries mainly as watchtowers.
column2: 中国人用砖或石材建塔，塔内设有楼梯；在后来的几个世纪里，这些塔主要用作瞭望塔。
column6: in later centuries|在后来的几个世纪里

column1: When the pagoda reached Japan, however, its architecture was freely adapted to local conditions - they were built less high, typically five rather than nine storeys, made mainly of wood and the staircase was dispensed with because the Japanese pagoda did not have any practical use but became more of an art object.
column2: 然而，佛塔传到日本后，建筑形式因地制宜，有了大幅调整。日本佛塔造得较矮，通常为五层而非九层，主要用木材建造，楼梯也被省去了。这是因为日本佛塔没有实际用途，更像是一件艺术品。

column1: Because of the typhoons that batter Japan in the summer, Japanese builders learned to extend the eaves of buildings further beyond the walls.
column2: 由于日本夏季常遭台风猛袭，当地工匠学会了把屋檐向墙外伸得更远。

column1: This prevents rainwater gushing down the walls.
column2: 这样可以防止雨水沿着墙面急流而下。

column1: Pagodas in China and Korea have nothing like the overhang that is found on pagodas in Japan.
column2: 中国和韩国的佛塔，屋檐都远没有日本佛塔挑出得那么长。
column3: have nothing like|远没有可与……相比的
column4: overhang|n. 屋檐向外挑出的部分

column1: The roof of a Japanese temple building can be made to overhang the sides of the structure by fifty per cent or more of the building’s overall width.
column2: 日本寺院建筑的屋顶可从侧面向外挑出，距离可达建筑总宽度的一半或更多。

column1: For the same reason, the builders of Japanese pagodas seem to have further increased their weight by choosing to cover these extended eaves not with the porcelain tiles of many Chinese pagodas but with much heavier earthenware tiles.
column2: 出于同样的原因，建造日本佛塔的工匠似乎还让塔更重了。他们选择在这些挑出的屋檐上铺设比瓷瓦重得多的陶瓦；许多中国佛塔用的则是瓷瓦。
column3: For the same reason|出于同样的原因

column1: But this does not totally explain the great resilience of Japanese pagodas.
column2: 但这还不能完全解释日本佛塔为何如此经得住冲击。
column5: resilience|n. 承受冲击并恢复的能力

column1: Is the answer that, like a tall pine tree, the Japanese pagoda - with its massive trunk-like central pillar known as shinbashira - simply flexes and sways during a typhoon or earthquake?
column2: 答案会不会是这样：日本佛塔像一棵高大的松树，有一根树干般粗壮的中央立柱，称为“心柱”，在台风或地震中只是弯曲、摇摆？
column3: like a tall pine tree|像一棵高大的松树

column1: For centuries, many thought so.
column2: 几个世纪以来，许多人都是这样认为的。

column1: But the answer is not so simple because the startling thing is that the shinbashira actually carries no load at all.
column2: 但答案没这么简单。令人意外的是，心柱实际上完全不承重。

column1: In fact, in some pagoda designs, it does not even rest on the ground, but is suspended from the top of the pagoda - hanging loosely down through the middle of the building.
column2: 事实上，有些佛塔的心柱甚至不落地，而是悬挂在塔顶，从那里垂下，自由地穿过整座塔的中央。
column9: through the middle of|穿过……的中央

column1: The weight of the building is supported entirely by twelve outer and four inner columns.
column2: 整座塔的重量完全由十二根外柱和四根内柱支撑。

column1: And what is the role of the shinbashira, the central pillar?
column2: 那么，居中的这根心柱究竟起什么作用？

column1: The best way to understand the shinbashira’s role is to watch a video made by Shuzo Ishida, a structural engineer at Kyoto Institute of Technology.
column2: 要了解心柱的作用，最好看一段由京都工艺纤维大学结构工程师石田修三拍摄的视频。

column1: Mr. Ishida, known to his students as ‘Professor Pagoda’ because of his passion to understand the pagoda, has built a series of models and tested them on a ‘shake-table’ in his laboratory.
column2: 石田先生热衷于研究佛塔，学生们称他为“佛塔教授”。他制作了一系列模型，在实验室的振动台上进行测试。

column1: In short, the shinbashira was acting like an enormous stationary pendulum.
column2: 简而言之，心柱起到了一个巨大静止摆锤的作用。
column4: was acting like|起到类似……的作用

column1: The ancient craftsmen, apparently without the assistance of very advanced mathematics, seemed to grasp the principles that were, more than a thousand years later, applied in the construction of Japan’s first skyscraper.
column2: 古代工匠看来并未借助十分高深的数学，却似乎已经掌握了一些原理。一千多年后，人们把这些原理用于建造日本的第一座摩天楼。

column1: What those early craftsmen had found by trial and error was that under pressure a pagoda’s loose stack of floors could be made to slither to and fro independent of one another.
column2: 那些早期工匠经过反复试验发现，塔身受力时，松松叠在一起的各层可以彼此独立地来回滑动。
column4: by trial and error|通过反复试验
column7: stack|n. 叠放在一起的一组
column11: independent of one another|彼此独立

column1: Viewed from the side, the pagoda seemed to be doing a snake dance - with each consecutive floor moving in the opposite direction to its neighbours above and below.
column2: 从侧面看，塔仿佛在跳蛇舞，每一层都朝着与其上下相邻楼层相反的方向移动。
column3: Viewed from the side|从侧面看

column1: The shinbashira, running up through a hole in the centre of the building, constrained individual storeys from moving too far because, after moving a certain distance, they banged into it, transmitting energy away along the column.
column2: 心柱从建筑中央的孔洞中向上贯穿，限制各层的移动幅度。这是因为每一层移到一定距离后便会碰到心柱，能量便沿着柱子传走。
column6: moving too far|移动幅度过大

column1: Another strange feature of the Japanese pagoda is that, because the building tapers, with each successive floor plan being smaller than the one below, none of the vertical pillars that carry the weight of the building is connected to its corresponding pillar above.
column2: 日本佛塔还有一个奇特之处。由于塔身向上逐渐收窄，每层的平面都比下一层小，承重的竖柱没有一根与上层对应的柱子相连。

column1: In other words, a five-storey pagoda contains not even one pillar that travels right up through the building to carry the structural loads from the top to the bottom.
column2: 换句话说，在一座五层佛塔里，连一根从顶到底贯通全塔、把上部结构荷载传到塔底的柱子都没有。
column5: not even one|连一个也没有
column7: right up through|一直向上贯穿
column9: from the top to the bottom|从顶部到底部

column1: More surprising is the fact that the individual storeys of a Japanese pagoda, unlike their counterparts elsewhere, are not actually connected to each other.
column2: 更令人惊讶的是，日本佛塔各层之间实际上互不相连，这和其他地方的同类佛塔不同。
column6: counterparts|n. 别处佛塔的对应楼层

column1: They are simply stacked one on top of another like a pile of hats.
column2: 各层只是一个叠一个地摞着，就像一摞帽子。
column5: one on top of another|一个叠在另一个上面

column1: Interestingly, such a design would not be permitted under current Japanese building regulations.
column2: 有意思的是，按照日本现行的建筑法规，这样的设计不会获准采用。

column1: And the extra-wide eaves?
column2: 那格外宽大的屋檐又有什么作用？

column1: Think of them as a tightrope walker’s balancing pole.
column2: 可以把这些屋檐想象成走钢丝者手中的平衡杆。
column3: Think of them as|把……想象成

column1: The bigger the mass at each end of the pole, the easier it is for the tightrope walker to maintain his or her balance.
column2: 平衡杆两端的质量越大，走钢丝的人就越容易保持平衡。

column1: The same holds true for a pagoda.
column2: 同样的道理也适用于佛塔。

column1: ‘With the eaves extending out on all sides like balancing poles,’ says Mr Ishida, ‘the building responds to even the most powerful jolt of an earthquake with a graceful swaying, never an abrupt shaking.’
column2: “屋檐像平衡杆一样向四面伸出，”石田先生说，“哪怕地震带来最猛烈的冲击，塔身也会舒缓地摇摆，绝不会猛地一晃。”

column1: Here again, Japanese master builders of a thousand years ago anticipated concepts of modern structural engineering.
column2: 这也表明，现代结构工程的某些理念，日本的建筑名匠在一千年前就已想到。
column3: Here again|从这一点也可以看出
column7: modern structural engineering|现代结构工程
